paragraphs: Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok. (a) Mishnah references (chapter:mishnah): Pe'ah 2:4. Kilayim 7:2, in Meir’s name. Shevi'it 2:4. Ma'aserot 4:4. Pesachim 3:6;10:3. Rosh Hashanah 2:7; folio 24a. Sanhedrin 7:2. Eduyot 2:5. Menachot 9:2. Chullin 3:6. Me'ilah 3:7. Middot 3:8. Kelim 2:5;26:9. Niddah 8:4. Mikvaot 6:10. Tohorot 2:8. Uktzin 1:6;2:7. Pesachim 49a,114a; Niddah 48b; Sanhedrin 71.

(b) Semag, negative commandment 235 (I did not find it), says he was a priest. Yuchasin, chronological section on priests under Tzadok: proof from Berakhot, Mi Shemeto 19b, where Elazar son of Tzadok says, “We leaped over coffins of the dead”—in a cemetery—to greet Israel’s kings. Rashi: he was a priest, as Bekhorot 36; likewise Tosafot, and Ketubbot 4b. Nachmanides writes: actual coffins, against which a priest is not warned. This proves nothing: perhaps they ate ordinary food in purity, being strict except for a commandment such as greeting kings. Kol Habbasar 107 and Mishnah Sukkah 2, 26b: Tzadok ate less than an egg outside the sukkah, wrapping his hands in cloth instead of washing. Tosafot: he was a priest, for a cloth is permitted to terumah eaters. No proof: they ate ordinary food in purity. Yevamot 15, beginning of b: Elazar son of Tzadok said, “Studying with Yochanan Hachorani, I saw him eating dry bread in famine and told Father. ‘Take olives,’ he said. Seeing them moist, he refused,” etc. Tosafot: Yochanan feared Tzadok did not guard against common people’s contact; though Tzadok was a priest, the clothes of scrupulous people count as impure by treading for terumah eaters, etc.—to teach that he ate ordinary food in purity. Bekhorot 36a [printed: 96a], the firstborn owned by Tzadok (Rashi: a priest), is no proof: an Israelite may buy it to await a blemish, or receive it as a gift. Nazir 44a: Tzadok’s father died in Ginzak. (Our reading: Yitzchak’s father; Semachot and Mo'ed Katan 20, end of a: Tzadok’s father, and they asked Elisha ben Avuya; see there.) He was told after three years and asked Yehoshua ben Elisha and four elders: “He may become impure for his father whole, not incomplete.” Thus he was a priest, if this is that Tzadok. Middot, chapter 3, and Gid Hannasheh: the golden vine in the Temple; Elazar son of Tzadok says three hundred priests were counted to move it. Why did he testify, except as a priest? Lulav va-Aravah 49: Elazar son of Tzadok says there was an opening in the altar where priests descended after seventy years, etc. No proof either: bringing Temple wood, they knew its affairs. Yoma 23a: two priests ascended the altar; one stabbed the other in the belly. Tzadok stood on the porch’s steps on the Temple Mount: “Hear: If a slain man is found in the land,” etc. Why did he expound unless he saw it as a priest? Again no proof: an elderly, respected, pious man, no priest would expound before him. Evidence against priesthood, agreeing with Maimonides’ omission from the priest list: Ta'anit 12a, Shekalim, and Bakkol Me'arvin 41a: Elazar son of Tzadok says, “I descended from Sena'av ben Binyamin. Nine Av fell on Shabbat; we postponed to ten Av and did not complete the fast, for it is our festival.” Rashi: a Benjaminite family allotted ten Av in Ezra’s time, hence their festival. Rosh, beginning of Makom Shenahagu: his fathers brought the wood-offering on ten Av. He lived after the destruction (likewise Tosafot in Ta'anit), but their whole family continued the festival. Tosafot: though a priest, perhaps his mother was Benjaminite, or he was their son-in-law and joined their company. End quotation. Second evidence against priesthood: Adam ve-Chavvah, mourning laws, path 28: “Elazar son of Tzadok: Father at death told me, First bury me in the valley; later gather my bones into a proper ossuary. Do not gather them yourself, lest they be contemptible in your eyes,” etc. “I did so. Yochanan entered, gathered them, and spread a cloth over them; I entered and tore my clothes.” Semachot, chapter 12, ends, “As he did for his father, so I did for him.” (They buried in earth, gathered bones, then buried in coffins.) Thus apparently not a priest: a priest becomes impure only for the whole body, not bones; see above. Why warn him against contempt? See Tzadok and what is written there.

(c) He saw the destruction and lived in Meir’s time, speaking in Meir’s name, Mishnah Kilayim 7:2. But Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 7:2 (Arba Mitot) [printed: ד׳ מידות], teaches capital jurisdiction ceased forty years before the destruction (likewise the beginning of chapter 1 there). Elazar son of Tzadok said, “I was a child riding Father’s shoulder; I saw a priest’s daughter who committed adultery surrounded with vine branches and burned.” They replied, “You were a child; a child’s testimony is no testimony.” Thus far also Babylonian Sanhedrin 52b. Jerusalem Talmud: “He was no younger than ten on seeing it. When walking with Rabbi he was no younger than thirty: a great man does not normally walk with someone under thirty. Rabbi said: Elazar son of Tzadok and I came from Beit Sharyon, eating figs and grapes casually outside a sukkah.” End quotation. Puzzling: his father was old at the destruction, fasting forty years beforehand; how was his son thirty a hundred years afterward, in Rabbi’s days? More: ten at the burning, which must precede the forty-year cessation, makes him at least fifty at the destruction. Akiva died fifty-two or seventy-three years afterward; Rabbi was born on Akiva’s death day. How was he thirty walking with Rabbi? Even accepting Tosafot, Sanhedrin, that they sometimes returned and judged within those forty years, a child of ten near the destruction could hardly be thirty in Rabbi’s time. Further, he studied under Yochanan ben Hachoranit, already old in Temple days: Beit Shammai’s and Beit Hillel’s elders visited him, and those houses preceded the destruction. Elazar son of Tzadok lived in Gamliel of Yavneh’s time, Yehoshua’s disputant, as Rashi, end of Bakkol Me'arvin. Tosefta and Jerusalem Talmud, end of Beitzah, chapter 2: “I often ate at Gamliel’s house”; Beitzah 22b: “I often entered Gamliel’s house after Father”; Pesachim 37a: “Once I entered after Father”;49a: “Father once spent Shabbat in Yavneh; fourteen Nisan fell on Shabbat. Zunin, Gamliel’s official, said it was time to remove leaven; I followed Father.” “When we intercalated the year at Yavneh,” Shabbat 11a; end of Beitzah, chapter 3. Jerusalem Talmud says he and Abba Shaul ben Batnit filled measures before festivals. Tosefta, end of Megillah, chapter 2: Yehudah says Elazar son of Tzadok bought the Alexandrians’ synagogue in Jerusalem and used it as he wished. All suggests an early man before Rabbi. I thought perhaps two: one in Rabbi’s time, the Kilayim 7 reporter of Meir, Rabbi’s teacher. Another proof: Sukkah 44b, Ivo stood before Elazar son of Tzadok; Rashi: Ivo, Rav’s father. Rav studied with Rabbi; his father Ivo therefore lived in Rabbi’s time, as did Elazar son of Tzadok. Thus two are necessary. Yuchasin instead writes Ivo stood before Elazar son of Yitzchak, with a willow beaten without blessing. Perhaps he felt this chronological difficulty and read Yitzchak. But Sukkah has Elazar son of Tzadok with Ivo in three matters, and Asheri and Tur, Orach Chayyim 664, also read Tzadok in the willow account. Hard to emend all as the same accidental error. Nor will you find Elazar son of Yitzchak throughout the Talmud; see the amoraim. Some support for two from Zohar, Vayetze, I 149a [printed locator: עשמ״ו]: Tzadok is called weak from fasting forty years against destruction; his grandson Tzadok the younger was with Shimon bar Yochai, with grown sons at the latter’s son’s wedding [in the Zohar, Tzadok Zuta speaks of his own son’s wedding]. Perhaps one was called Elazar son of Tzadok the younger. Ivo’s standing before him would fit: Rav son of Ivo is Zohar’s Rabbi Abba, Shimon bar Yochai’s student (see Abba Arikha). But Tosefta Sukkah, chapter 2: Rabbi said, “Elazar son of Tzadok and I once went to Yochanan ben Nuri at Beit She'arim, eating grapes outside the sukkah.” The above Jerusalem Talmud omits Yochanan ben Nuri. He was Yehoshua and Gamliel’s colleague—Gamliel, Rabbi’s grandfather. Eruvin 11b: Yehoshua went to learn with him, calling him “my teacher.” How could Rabbi be with Elazar son of Tzadok in their time? The truth: Tosefta and Jerusalem Talmud refer to unqualified Rabban Gamliel, Gamliel of Yavneh, as “Rabbi” (see his entry). Thus one, not two. Jerusalem Talmud’s thirty-year-old walking with Rabbi means, according to Yuchasin, Gamliel of Yavneh, appointed three or four years after the destruction. Tzadok lived several years afterward too: Eikhah Rabbah, “Their appearance darker than black,” Elazar son of Tzadok says, “Though Father lived all those years afterward, his body never recovered.” End quotation. Necessarily his age ten at the burning follows Tosafot: they sometimes judged capital cases within the forty years after leaving the Hewn Chamber. He could thus be thirty in “Rabbi’s,” meaning Gamliel of Yavneh’s, days. Ivo stood before him because Rav is Abba, Shimon bar Yochai’s student; Shimon was a student when Gamliel was removed after three or four years as nasi and they sought to appoint Elazar ben Azaryah, Berakhot. No wonder Elazar son of Tzadok lived in Rav’s father Ivo’s time. Tosefta, Berakhot, chapter 2, and Sanhedrin, chapter 8: “When Gamliel sat in Yavneh’s court, Father”—Jerusalem Talmud, end of Sanhedrin, chapter 1: “Father and his brother”—“sat at his right, elders at his left.” Elazar son of Tzadok says Father brought two incidents from Tiv'in, asked the sages, who asked physicians, Niddah 22b. He saw Nakdimon ben Guryon’s daughter gathering barley among horses’ hoofs, Ketubbot 67a, and saw her hair tied to a horse’s tail as she was driven from Jerusalem to Lod, Eikhah Rabbah [which names Miriam bat Boethus in this second account].
Yuchasin, Yesod Olam in Rema’s glosses: “Yochanan ben Zakkai’s colleagues: Tzadok and his son Elazar.” Elazar son of Tzadok being Zakkai’s colleague requires examination; it is improbable.

(d) Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok. In Rabban Gamliel’s name, Pe'ah, chapter 2. Rav Yehudah said in Shmuel’s name, from Elazar son of Tzadok, Bekhorot 22a. Rabbi Yochanan: “I received from Elazar son of Tzadok.” In Meir’s name, Kilayim (see above). Shimon ben Elazar from Elazar son of Tzadok. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Chanina bar Chanina (see there).
